readingInstruction: Read Mark 13:1-37. Jesus predicts the destruction of the temple, speaks of tribulation and false teachers, and describes the coming of the Son of Man. The call throughout is to stay awake. Read it for its pastoral purpose.
settingTheScene: As Jesus leaves the temple, a disciple marvels at the huge stones and buildings. Jesus says that not one stone will be left on another. Later, on the Mount of Olives, four disciples ask, “When will these things be, and what will be the sign?” His answer is the Olivet Discourse. It is one of the most debated passages in the Bible. It seems to speak both of the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70 and of the return of Christ at the end, and interpreters differ on how to divide the two.
observation: “Do you see these great buildings? There will not be left here one stone upon another that will not be thrown down” (13:2).
“And when you hear of wars and rumors of wars, do not be alarmed. This must take place, but the end is not yet” (13:7).
“And the gospel must first be proclaimed to all nations” (13:10).
“And you will be hated by all for my name’s sake. But the one who endures to the end will be saved” (13:13).
“And then they will see the Son of Man coming in clouds with great power and glory” (13:26).
“Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (13:31).
“But concerning that day or that hour, no one knows, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father” (13:32).
“And what I say to you I say to all: Stay awake” (13:37).
interpretation:
Jesus tells the disciples not to be led astray. Many will come in his name, saying “I am he.” Wars and rumors of wars, earthquakes, and famines are “the beginning of the birth pains,” not the end. The disciples will be handed over to councils and beaten in synagogues, and will stand before governors and kings for Jesus’ sake, “to bear witness before them.” The gospel must be proclaimed to all nations. When they are arrested, they are not to worry about what to say, for the Holy Spirit will speak through them. Families will be divided, and they will be hated for his name’s sake. “But the one who endures to the end will be saved.”

Then he speaks of the “abomination of desolation” standing where it ought not to be, a phrase from Daniel. When it appears, those in Judea should flee to the mountains. There will be a tribulation such as has not been since the beginning of creation. This language fits the Roman siege of Jerusalem in AD 70, when the temple was destroyed, and many see a further fulfillment in a final tribulation. He warns again about false christs and false prophets who perform signs.

After that tribulation, the sun will be darkened, the moon will not give its light, and the stars will fall. This is the language of cosmic upheaval, used in the prophets for the fall of nations and the day of the LORD. “And then they will see the Son of Man coming in clouds with great power and glory.” This echoes Daniel 7:13. He will send out the angels and gather his elect from the four winds.

Jesus then gives a lesson from the fig tree: when you see its leaves, you know that summer is near. So when you see these things, know that he is near. “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.” The time of the end is hidden: not even the Son knows it, only the Father. Jesus speaks here of his human knowledge.

The conclusion is not a timetable but a command: stay awake. A man going on a journey puts his servants in charge, and commands the doorkeeper to be on watch. The master may come in the evening, at midnight, at cockcrow, or in the morning. “Lest he come suddenly and find you asleep.” It is a call to faithful readiness, not speculation. And note that in the very next chapters, the disciples fall asleep in Gethsemane.
connection: Daniel 7:13-14, 9:27, 11:31, and 12:11 are the background to the abomination of desolation and the Son of Man. Isaiah 13:10 and 34:4 use the language of cosmic signs. Joel 2:10 and 2:31 describe the sun and moon darkened. Matthew 24 and 25 and Luke 21 parallel this discourse. 1 Thessalonians 5:1-11 teaches readiness for the day of the Lord. 2 Peter 3:3-13 warns of scoffers and urges holy living. Revelation 1:7 echoes the coming with the clouds.
application:
Ask whether you are awake or asleep, spiritually. What would it look like to be ready?

When news of wars and disasters comes, remember: “This must take place, but the end is not yet.” Do not be alarmed.

Hold the date-setters at arm’s length, as Jesus did. Focus on faithfulness in your assigned work.
prayerPrompts: Ask Jesus to keep you watchful.
Thank him that his words will never pass away.
Ask him to keep you from being deceived.
